highlights.annotation: A word counts only when no identifier character follows it, so `pub` never matches the start of a longer word.
The name is the identifier right after one of the keywords.
A Rust `fn` is a function, a `const` a value; each calls the helpers shown above.
Python needs only `def` and `class`, after stepping over `async`.

prompt.content: A lesson shows `fn key(...)`. Later code contains `let key = 1;` and `key(queue)`. Which of the two `key` names link to the definition?

choices.explanation: A function definition only links usages that are calls; the variable merely shares the name.

choices.content: Both, since the names are the same
choices.explanation: Linking both would send the learner from an unrelated variable to the function.

hints: What kind does `fn` give a definition, and which usages does that kind accept?
blocks.explanation: `fn key` is a function, and functions only link where they are called. The variable `key` stays plain; the call links.

highlights.annotation: Parentheses and braces are counted outside strings and comments; `;` ends a definition only before any body.
A closed body ends the definition; in Go and shell a line without `{` is a whole definition.

prompt.content: A Rust function's parameters span four lines before its `{`. Where does its recorded extent end?

choices.content: At the closing brace of its body
At the end of its first line
choices.explanation: That is what a three-line lookahead used to give; parentheses are now tracked until the body opens.

choices.content: At the fortieth line after it
choices.explanation: Forty lines is only the cap; the extent ends as soon as the body's braces balance.

hints: What stops a `;` or a line break from ending the definition early?
blocks.explanation: While parentheses are open, the signature continues; once `{` opens the body, the definition ends where the braces balance again.

highlights.annotation: Each line either starts a definition or not; the extent is found from there.
What follows the name decides the usage: `(` is a call, `!` a macro.
The definition's own line never links, and each kind accepts only its usages.

prompt.content: The text `// call key(queue) here` sits in a comment. Does `key` link?

choices.content: No, comments are skipped before any matching
Yes, because it is followed by a parenthesis
choices.explanation: The call test only runs on names outside comment and string tokens.

choices.content: Only when the lesson shows one definition
choices.explanation: Uniqueness only matters for names in code; comment text never gets that far.

hints: Which highlight.js tokens does the marking step skip?
blocks.explanation: highlight.js puts the comment in its own token, which the marking step skips entirely, so nothing inside it links.

highlights.annotation: Only Cmd or Ctrl turns a click into a jump; a plain click still selects text.
One definition jumps right away; several open the chooser, pinned until closed.

prompt.content: A lesson shows two `new` methods. What happens on Cmd/Ctrl+click of a call to `new`?

choices.content: A chooser lists both definitions to pick from
The browser jumps to the first definition shown
choices.explanation: Guessing would often pick the wrong one, so several sites open a chooser.

choices.content: Nothing happens, since the name is ambiguous
choices.explanation: Staying silent was the fallback; the chooser keeps the name useful.

hints: How many sites does the mark carry?
blocks.explanation: Both `new` sites are listed, each with a preview and a button, and the learner picks one.
